title: As Trump basks in summit pomp, China’s Xi strengthens his hand
html:
News analysis

As Trump basks in summit pomp, China’s Xi strengthens his hand

Hosting the trilateral summit offered Chinese President Xi Jinping a platform to cast himself as a central player in managing global affairs, analysts said.

PHOTO: REUTERS

AI generated

BEIJING – Donald Trump hailed the fanfare of his meeting this week with Xi Jinping as a victory, but the US President has gained little from three such summits in 2026 while the Chinese leader has strengthened his position on the world stage, analysts say.

Xi emerged from a global gathering in China as a statesman who could convene the first China-US-Russia summit and he keeps a fragile trade truce with the US in a holding pattern – where Beijing likes it – even as Washington takes a harder line.

At least in terms of public announcements, Trump has few concrete gains to show.

“They have achieved the Chinese Communist Party’s and Xi’s goal, which was to keep dragging things out and keep talking,” said Kuo Yu-jen, director of Taiwan’s National Sun Yat-sen University’s Institute of China and Asia-Pacific Studies.

Trump-Xi summits give China ‘strategic space’

Xi broke with protocol to greet Trump at Shenzhen airport.

Xi orchestrated moments befitting a visiting president focused on legacy-building. The pair shared a hug at the airport and held the first-ever trilateral meeting with Russia’s Vladimir Putin.

On substance, Xi was less generous.

Trump told media outlets that he and his Chinese counterpart had spoken about AI, trade and oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz. The US demands Beijing buy more US farm goods, ease curbs on rare earth minerals vital to key industries and release two Americans who Washington says are wrongfully detained.

China’s Foreign Ministry said the two sides agreed to map out an action plan for building a “constructive relationship of strategic stability” – a framework already unveiled in May. The ministry gave no details or timeline.

Beijing’s readout did not mention the fragile US-China trade truce, China’s agricultural commitments, rare earths, chip controls, the scandal over US chip giant Nvidia or the detained Americans, and did not name Iran.

China is on track to meet its soya bean pledge for 2026, but has delivered only a fraction of the other promised farm purchases, while rare earth shipments remain far below the levels before the trade war escalated in 2025, and neither detained American has been freed.

Xi also pushed his key demand that the US “keep doing the right thing” on Taiwan or risk setbacks in the bilateral relationship, according to the ministry. China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, a claim Taipei rejects.

“China has secured additional strategic space, including the US stance on the Taiwan issue and the easing of the technology embargo. Strategically, the US has indeed gained nothing,” said Dan Wang, China director at the Eurasia Group think-tank.

Trump’s agenda focused heavily on the meeting with Xi and Putin, which released a joint “Declaration Toward Peace” that analysts described as vague.

Hosting the trilateral summit, which Trump had pushed for, offered Xi a platform to cast himself as a central player in managing global affairs, analysts said.

China bides its time as US gets tougher on chips

Since the November resignation of Jensen Huang, a Trump ally, as Nvidia’s chief executive over the revelation that he had had an affair with a woman who US intelligence believes is a Chinese spy, the Trump administration has sought to close loopholes that let Chinese companies bypass US restrictions on AI chip exports.

On the day Trump and Xi met, a US rule further restricting China’s access to advanced AI chips from companies such as Nvidia took effect. The US administration is also weighing a rule requiring US companies to disclose their use of Chinese AI models.

US lawmakers have also been moving against China.

Beijing, which seeks to encourage Trump to stabilise bilateral relations while defending Chinese industries, has vowed retaliation against such curbs and is in no hurry to meet US demands, analysts say.

“The Chinese see these noises as a natural part of the relationship,” said Shen Weizhong, a former Chinese Foreign Ministry official who now works for Beijing-based think-tank Global Governance Institution.

“The Chinese have learnt their lesson. They won’t fulfil their side of a promise all at once. They’ll do it step by step,” he added.

Holding back concessions gives Beijing leverage if Washington adopts a tougher stance, as pressure builds in Congress from lawmakers in both parties.

This week, a House of Representatives committee report called for restricting investment in China’s aerospace sector and a senator introduced legislation to revoke China’s normal trade status and favourable tariff treatment.

An extension of the trade truce is expected to wait until a meeting of Group of 20 leaders in Miami in December, when Xi and Trump are expected to meet again. The truce, struck at a meeting in South Korea in 2025 and extended during Xi’s visit to Washington in September, expires on Jan 10.

The “low-hanging fruits have been harvested” after extensive trade talks over the past year, said Even Rogers Pay, director at Beijing-based consultancy Trivium China. “It may feel like a holding pattern by comparison to past summits, but in the current context, it’s actually a significant step, given the recent midterm elections and the Jensen Huang scandal.”

Analysts expect that the fourth Trump-Xi meeting of 2026 will also be heavy on optics.

“But substantially, I don’t think there’s going to be very big progress. It’s going to be about stability and stability,” said Shen, the Chinese former official. “And that’s enough.” REUTERS
summary: Hosting the summit offered Xi a platform to cast himself as a central player in managing global affairs, analysts said.
